questions.problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{3}$ if $f(x)=11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =11(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\sqrt{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ if $f(x) = \dfrac{-2\cot x}{\sin x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{-2\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-2\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-2(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+2\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\sqrt{2})+2\cdot (1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions are shown in the table below:

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\sec x$ | $\sec x\tan x$ |
| $\csc x$ | $-\csc x\cot x$ |
| $\cot x$ | $-\csc^2 x$ |

As with the standard trigonometric functions, we can now differentiate any combination of the above functions using the rules of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of 

$$
y= \sec x + \csc x.
$$

We can take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We could have computed the derivative of the above function by rewriting it as

$$
y= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{1}{\sin x}
$$

and applying the appropriate derivative rules. However, this would have taken significantly more work! You can save a lot of time by memorizing the derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions.

tutorials.name: Mnemonic Tricks
tutorials.problem:
Trigonometric functions appear very frequently in calculus, so it's extremely important to commit their derivatives to memory.

Conveniently, there are some mnemonic tricks that we can use to more easily remember the derivatives of trigonometric functions.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x) & =-{csc}^{2}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}⁡x) & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the "co"-functions (cosine, cosecant, and cotangent) all have negative signs in their derivatives, while the other trigonometric functions (sine, secant, and tangent) do not.

It's also helpful to realize that functions come in pairs.

- Sine and cosine are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Tangent and secant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Cotangent and cosecant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

Lastly, it's helpful to realize the following:

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, tangent and cotangent have a similar format for their derivatives: the square of the function they're paired with.

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, secant and cosecant have a similar format for their derivatives: the product of themself and the function they're paired with.

tutorials.name: Justifying the Derivatives of Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions
tutorials.problem:
To see why the derivative of $\sec x$ is $\sec x \tan x,$ we start by remembering that

$$
\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}.
$$

If we now differentiate the above relation using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x-1\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{{[\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(0)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x-1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={{\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{{\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the same method to find the derivative of the other two reciprocal trigonometric functions,

$$
\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}.
$$
